paragraphs.source_en: To seventeenth-century Ottoman historians, manliness and male virtue were central in the making and unmaking of sultans.! Prior to the modern era, Ottoman writers, like writers in the rest of Europe, did not distinguish between masculinity and femininity. Instead, in Renaissance Europe and the Ottoman Empire, authors judged people by their male or female virtues 270 THE OTTOMANS and performance of gendered positions. In the Ottoman Empire, manliness was defined by bravery and courage proven on the battlefield—labelled interchangeably gaza or jihad. To understand what this meant for Ottoman sultans, we only need consider the reigns of Ibrahim I (reigned 1640-1648) and Mehmed IV (reigned 1648-1687).

paragraphs.source_en: Following Mustafa I’s second deposition, when he was sent to the harem to while away the rest of his days in 1623, Ahmed I’s eldest surviving son, the eleven-year-old Murad, replaced him as Murad IV (reigned 1623-1640) on the throne. Murad IV was overshadowed for the first ten years of his reign by his regent, favourite of Ahmed I and mother of the sultan Késem Sultan. In these years, the Ottomans lost Baghdad to the Safavids in 1624 and Murad IV failed to take it back in 1630. He managed to reconquer Yerevan, Armenia, in 1635 and retook Baghdad in 1638. After the first conquest, he had his brothers Bayezid and Suleiman put to death; after the second, it was the turn of his brother Kasim.? To commemorate his military feats, he built the stunningly beautiful, octagonal, blue-tiled Baghdad and Yerevan pleasure pavilions in the fourth courtyard at Topkapi Palace.
